title: Efficient Estimation of Reduced QAOA Expressibility on Acyclic Graphs
abstract: Classically equivalent formulations of an optimization problem need not lead to equivalent quantum algorithms. For MaxCut, fixing the value of a single vertex removes a simple global symmetry without changing the underlying optimization problem, yet it can substantially alter the quantum dynamics generated by the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). These dynamics are captured by the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra (DLA), whose direct construction can become exponentially expensive. Here we show that, for symmetry-reduced QAOA on trees, substantial information about the reduced DLA can instead be obtained efficiently from the graph alone. We introduce a polynomial classical algorithm that recursively distinguishes vertices using shortest path structure and degree parity. When all vertices are resolved individually, the method determines the complete reduced DLA and, under the corresponding graph conditions, certifies maximal expressibility of the reduced QAOA ansatz. Even when full resolution is not achieved, the algorithm identifies embedded subalgebras, provides rigorous lower bounds on DLA dimension, and certifies controllable subsystems. Our theoretical and experimental results show how classical graph structure can be used to diagnose and potentially guide the quantum dynamics of variational algorithms before running them on quantum hardware.

title: Low-Cost Model Selection for Transformers (LoCoMoSeT)
abstract: The wide availability of performant pre-trained models in online repositories, such as the HuggingFace model hub, has led to a paradigm shift in applied data science away from training new models from scratch and towards transfer learning–fine-tuning existing pre-trained models on a new downstream task of interest.

title: Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence: A Review of Transformative Technologies and Applications
abstract: The current trends in Artificial Intelligence technologies continually transform multiple business sectors while changing how humans connect with machines. Contemporary technology views AI as its essential component instead of remaining as a separate specialized study field. A review of primary AI trends coupled with applications and obstacles in modern AI research served as the focus of this academic paper. Healthcare decision transparency integrates with financial needs to enable smart infrastructure deployment by connecting Explainable AI (XAI) with Federated Learning under Edge Computing framework. The barriers to progress include major issues with scalability together with interoperability standards and ethical needs for organizational governance. Interdisciplinary teamwork constitutes an absolute requirement to construct responsible AI systems together with dependable deployment frameworks as demonstrated through the term paper. The review combines recent research findings with guidance on new investigation tracks for developing all-encompassing AI systems which both spread far-reaching outcomes and follow sustainability requirements.

title: The Case for AI-Assisted Learning in Elementary Education
abstract: A research-based brief for parents and educators of elementary-age children (grades 3-5, ages 8-10). Synthesizes cognitive psychology, meta-analyses of intelligent tutoring systems, and randomized controlled trials to make the case for well-designed AI use in a 4th grader's schoolwork.

title: Reproducibility package for: A Cross-Silo Experimental Framework for Federated Voice Deepfake Detection: Heterogeneity, Poisoning, and Update-Cancellation Diagnostics
abstract: Data, code, results, and provenance package for the article “A Cross-Silo Experimental Framework for Federated Voice Deepfake Detection: Heterogeneity, Poisoning, and Update-Cancellation Diagnostics.” The package contains recovered original Linear-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (LFCC)/WavLM notebooks, model checkpoints, training histories, poisoning/defense histories, score files, and automated artifact and Equal Error Rate (EER) verification, together with a fully specified 20-seed controlled update-cancellation experiment, independent-and-identically-distributed (IID)/non-IID heterogeneity ablations, defense-sensitivity analyses, attack-weight controls, reference outputs, figures, and reproduction instructions. The package documents both the archived original audio experiment and a controlled mechanism-replication experiment designed to isolate update cancellation and stress-test robust-aggregation assumptions. The latter is a synthetic mechanistic experiment and is not presented as external audio validation. The associated journal manuscript is intentionally not included in this archive. Copyrighted ASVspoof audio, large rebuildable feature caches, and third-party pretrained WavLM weights are not redistributed. The archived notebooks document how the derived feature representations can be regenerated from the publicly available source datasets. The package supports direct verification of the reported archived artifacts and reproducibility of the controlled numerical experiments. Exact bitwise-identical retraining of the historical audio experiment is not claimed because the original software environment was not fully pinned.

title: Adaptive Geometric Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of adaptive geometric quantum entanglement to simulate topological structures and unlock new capabilities in quantum computing and information processing. The core concept revolves around leveraging quantum entanglement to mimic the intricate geometry of topological phases, providing a novel approach to system optimization and understanding. We investigate the mechanisms by which this simulation can lead to enhanced performance and the unique advantages of this approach. The research focuses on the application of quantum entanglement to generate and analyze topological configurations, ultimately aiming to address limitations of current quantum computation methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Optimization via Dynamic Quantum Algorithm Tuning
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization approach for quantum algorithms leveraging dynamic quantum algorithm tuning. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter settings, limiting the potential for efficient algorithm execution. We introduce a dynamic mechanism that automatically adjusts the quantum algorithm's execution characteristics based on learned properties, resulting in accelerated quantum computation. The core of this method lies in a "dynamic quantum algorithm tuning" mechanism, which iteratively refines the algorithm's parameters to achieve optimal performance. This approach addresses the limitations of static optimization techniques by providing a flexible and adaptive optimization strategy. This research explores the potential of dynamically adjusting quantum algorithms to significantly enhance their computational speed.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的异质数据分布建模
abstract: This paper investigates the application of an adaptive neural network (ANN) framework for robust data distribution modeling. Traditional neural networks often rely on fixed, pre-defined parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle diverse data distributions. This research introduces a novel ANN architecture that dynamically adjusts its parameters based on the characteristics of the input data, resulting in improved model generalization and robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and experiments focusing on scenarios exhibiting varying data distributions. The core mechanism revolves around an adaptive parameter adjustment strategy, which leverages a feedback loop to continuously refine the network's response to changing data patterns. The results showcase a significant enhancement in model performance across a range of datasets, highlighting the potential for this approach in various data science applications.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainability via Differential Privacy and Data Auditing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to enhancing algorithmic transparency and explainability in machine learning models by integrating differential privacy and data auditing techniques. Traditional explainability methods often fall short in addressing fundamental concerns about data privacy and potential biases embedded within datasets. We propose a framework where differential privacy is applied to mitigate privacy risks during model training, while automated data auditing tools meticulously track data lineage and identify potential sources of bias. The core mechanism involves adding calibrated noise to training data and model parameters, ensuring statistical privacy guarantees. Simultaneously, data auditing tools provide a traceable record of data transformations and feature selection, facilitating accountability and allowing for the detection of unintended biases. This approach moves beyond simply explaining model outputs and focuses on establishing a robust system of transparency and accountability throughout the entire machine learning lifecycle. The proposed methodology offers a significant advancement in building trustworthy and responsible AI systems.

title: Non-Standard Quantum State Collapse – Bayesian-Guided Reconstruction
abstract: This paper explores the challenges and opportunities of quantum state collapse, specifically focusing on the need for adaptive reconstruction techniques. We propose a novel Bayesian-guided algorithm designed to address this challenge by incorporating a dynamically adjusted Bayesian network. The algorithm aims to reconstruct complex quantum states from sparse data, leveraging the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The core mechanism involves a Bayesian network that continuously refines the collapse process based on observed data, promoting a more robust and adaptable reconstruction. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, demonstrates its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and discusses its potential implications for various quantum computing applications.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Explainable Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) is a burgeoning field aiming to address the inherent "black-box" nature of traditional reinforcement learning (RL) agents, particularly deep neural networks. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to provide interpretable explanations for RL policies. The core idea is to represent the agent's knowledge of the environment and its actions within a DBN, allowing for explicit probabilistic reasoning. The agent's experience dynamically updates the DBN, leading to a transparent account of the policy decisions. Unlike traditional RL methods that primarily focus on reward optimization, this approach directly encodes and explains the reasoning process. We demonstrate the potential of this framework by outlining its construction and operation, highlighting its advantages in terms of interpretability and providing a foundation for future research. The key contribution lies in the explicit modeling of belief states and their evolution, offering a pathway to understand *why* an RL agent makes specific decisions.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Temporal Logic Programming
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neuro-symbolic reasoning that leverages temporal logic programming. The core idea is to bridge the gap between neural networks and symbolic reasoning by employing temporal logic to explicitly represent and reason about temporal dependencies within a system. We train a neural network to predict the truth value of temporal logic formulas, effectively translating neural network outputs into symbolic representations. These symbolic representations are then fed into a symbolic reasoning engine, allowing for the execution of complex reasoning tasks that would be difficult or impossible with purely neural or purely symbolic approaches. The system's architecture and training methodology are detailed, highlighting the benefits of this combined approach. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a theoretical framework, focusing on the integration of temporal logic and neural network predictions. The key innovation lies in the direct application of temporal logic as the interface between the neural and symbolic components, offering a more interpretable and controllable method for neuro-symbolic reasoning.

title: Formal Specification of Secure Multi-Party Computation Protocols
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) allows multiple parties to compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. However, ensuring the security of MPC protocols is a complex and challenging task. This paper presents a novel approach to formally specifying and verifying MPC protocols, leveraging mathematical frameworks like category theory to provide a rigorous foundation. We define key security properties using mathematical notation, focusing on completeness, soundness, and correctness. The core claim is that formal specifications significantly enhance the confidence in the security of MPC protocols by enabling automated verification. This work outlines a methodology for constructing formal models of MPC protocols, highlighting the benefits of a mathematically precise approach compared to traditional, informal security analyses. The detailed formulation and application of these specifications will contribute to the development of more robust and trustworthy MPC systems.

title: Quantum State Non-Linear Mapping and Topology Transformations
abstract: Quantum states exhibit remarkable sensitivity to their environment, making them ideal candidates for exploring novel quantum device designs. This paper investigates the interplay between non-linear mapping and topology transformations, proposing a novel algorithm for dynamically optimizing quantum device design based on the observed effects of these transformations. We analyze how non-linear mapping alters the topology of quantum states, leading to quantifiable changes in device performance. The core mechanism focuses on a specific mapping function, which is then optimized through iterative transformations. This research explores the potential for leveraging these transformations to achieve unprecedented device design precision and efficiency. The resulting design suggests a pathway toward the creation of highly tailored quantum devices with enhanced capabilities.

title: Dynamic Modular Quantum Computation for Non-Von Neumann Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum computing architecture termed "Dynamic Modular Quantum Computation" (DMQC) that fundamentally departs from the traditional Von Neumann architecture by eliminating the need for classical storage units. The core concept leverages quantum entanglement and dynamic module reconfiguration to achieve parallel quantum computation and efficient result aggregation. The architecture is built upon entangled quantum modules, where the degree of entanglement and module connectivity are dynamically controlled to orchestrate computations. This approach directly addresses the inherent storage limitations of Von Neumann architectures, offering a significantly more scalable and potentially more efficient pathway toward realizing practical quantum computation. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, key operational principles, and potential advantages of the DMQC architecture, highlighting its departure from conventional design paradigms. ---

title: Quantum Entanglement Encoding for Multi-Dimensional Data Compression
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to multi-dimensional data compression leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional compression methods often struggle to overcome the inherent limitations imposed by the Shannon entropy theorem, particularly when dealing with complex, high-dimensional data. Our proposed method utilizes the correlated nature of entangled quantum states to achieve superior compression ratios. We demonstrate a mapping of multi-dimensional data into a set of entangled quantum states, exploiting the instantaneous correlations between these states to represent the data efficiently. The core of the method lies in manipulating the entangled states to encode information, potentially exceeding the compression limits achievable with classical techniques. The theoretical framework is outlined, focusing on the key mathematical principles underpinning the entanglement-based compression process. This work explores the potential of quantum mechanics to revolutionize data compression, offering a new paradigm for handling vast datasets with unprecedented efficiency. The method is presented with a focus on the mathematical formulation and the underlying principles.

title: Probability Field Theory-Driven Computation: A Novel Framework for Quantum Computing Efficiency and Algorithm Design
abstract: Probability Field Theory (PFT) offers a powerful approach to quantum computing by leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement and the quantum spin. This paper investigates the application of PFT to drive computation, specifically focusing on the utilization of spin-dependent quantum gates to enhance quantum algorithm efficiency. We present a novel framework, "Self-Spin Dynamics," that employs a self-induced spin-state to facilitate quantum interference and entanglement, thereby optimizing the performance of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism involves the creation of self-oscillating spin states, which allow for the manipulation of quantum states with unprecedented precision. The paper explores the potential of this approach in addressing limitations inherent in traditional quantum computing and demonstrates preliminary results suggesting significant improvements in algorithm speed and accuracy. The investigation explores the impact of self-oscillating spin states on quantum circuit design and optimization, providing a pathway towards more efficient quantum computations.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Optimization of Constraint Programming
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to accelerate the solution of constraint programming problems. Traditional methods often struggle with the vast solution spaces, necessitating significant computational resources. We explore the application of quantum annealing and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to enhance the search process, aiming to significantly reduce the time required for optimization. The core mechanism involves leveraging quantum phenomena to overcome the limitations of classical algorithms, offering a promising avenue for improved performance in constraint programming. The research focuses on the theoretical advantages and potential practical implementations of these quantum approaches, specifically examining how they can be applied to benchmark problems and demonstrate a quantifiable speedup compared to traditional methods.

title: Dimension Space Information Theory Reinforcement Learning Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning framework based on dimension space information theory, designed to address the challenges of high-dimensional environments. We propose a method that leverages the inherent structure of high-dimensional spaces to guide exploration and learning, enabling the development of robust and optimal strategies. The core of this framework utilizes information theory principles to represent state spaces and action spaces, allowing for efficient and adaptive policy learning. The framework's innovation lies in its integration of both traditional reinforcement learning techniques and dimension space information theory, resulting in improved performance across a range of complex scenarios. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to learn complex strategies and achieve high rewards. The key contribution is a method for automatically discovering optimal policies within high-dimensional spaces, moving beyond the limitations of conventional approaches.

title: Quantum Entanglement Path Discovery – A Dynamic Path Exploration Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents unique opportunities for computation and information transfer. This paper investigates a novel quantum path discovery method leveraging the inherent dynamic properties of entangled states. We propose a framework that employs a continuous, iterative exploration of entangled quantum states, optimizing for a predefined objective function through a process of dynamic path adjustment. The core mechanism centers on exploiting entanglement to instantaneously correlate states and guide the exploration process. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional algorithms, particularly in scenarios demanding high efficiency and robustness. We detail the methodology, analyze its potential benefits, and present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this dynamic path discovery strategy.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Probability Space Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive probability space optimization algorithm designed to address the challenges of complex optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameters, limiting the algorithm's ability to effectively model and predict the outcomes of intricate optimization scenarios. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts probability space parameters, enabling a more nuanced and responsive optimization process. This approach enhances the algorithm's capacity to capture the inherent complexities within the problem domain, resulting in improved optimization quality and robustness. We detail the core mechanism, the design of the dynamic parameter adjustment process, and the resulting performance improvements compared to existing approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications and future research directions.

title: Pigeons That Learn to Flank You: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds in the context of Game Development. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of game AI and NPCs as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Game Development.

title: Soft Disagreement-Based Adaptive Uncertainty Regulation for Fuzzy Servo Control
authors: Dosti Kh. Abbas Dosti Kh. Abbas
abstract: This paper proposes a supervisory soft disagreement framework for adaptive uncertainty regulation in Interval Type-2 (IT2) fuzzy servo control and validates its performance through embedded implementation on an industrial servo platform. The proposed framework introduces a supervisory learning layer that combines supervised classification and unsupervised fuzzy clustering to characterize servo operating conditions using experimentally extracted performance indicators, including rise time, settling time, overshoot, steady-state error, Integral Absolute Error (IAE), control-effort energy, tracking-error standard deviation, and maximum control effort. Operating condition confidence is quantified by measuring the soft disagreement between the posterior class probabilities of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier and the normalized membership degrees of a Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering algorithm using the Bhattacharyya coefficient. The resulting disagreement index adaptively regulates the Footprint of Uncertainty (FOU) of the antecedent membership functions in IT2 fuzzy controller. A closed-form Uncertainty Avoider Defuzzification (UAD) strategy enables computationally efficient uncertainty-aware type reduction for real-time embedded implementation without iterative procedures. The framework was trained using experimental data collected from a Delta ASDA-B2 400 W industrial servo drive under diverse operating conditions. The complete controller was implemented on a Raspberry Pi and experimentally compared with conventional Proportional–Integral–Derivative (PID), Type-1, and fixed-FOU IT2 fuzzy controllers. Experimental results show that the proposed controller achieved an average IAE of 1.08, representing improvements of 55.6% and 27.5% over the PID and fixed-FOU IT2 controllers, respectively. Overshoot was reduced to 2.2% and settling time to 0.24 s, while the supervisory computation required only 4.55 ms, confirming real-time feasibility. The scientific significance of this work lies in introducing a new disagreement-driven supervisory paradigm that links probabilistic machine learning confidence with adaptive fuzzy uncertainty regulation. By establishing a principled connection among supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and Interval Type-2 fuzzy control, the proposed framework provides a general foundation for confidence-aware adaptive uncertainty management in intelligent control systems operating under uncertain and time-varying conditions.

title: PerfReasoning: How Well Do LLMs Reason on Hardware Performance?
abstract: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, yet constructing these models requires structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. We introduce PerfReasoning, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs both as direct performance reasoners and as generators of analytical performance-model code. Given workload, architecture, and mapping specifications, models compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. The strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%. However, model construction is substantially harder: while GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, all other model configurations average below 45% and vary markedly across runs. Task-specific RL raises a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision prompting is not reliably effective. PerfReasoning exposes the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. We will publicly release the benchmark to support reproducible evaluation and track future progress.

title: Toward Resilient Many-Body Formulations under Incomplete Correlation Models: A Dual-Space Variational Formulation
abstract: Quantum simulations of correlated many-body systems will inevitably operate with imperfect information: the prepared states may arise from incomplete or approximate ansatze, while their measured Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements are additionally affected by hardware and statistical noise. Robust quantum algorithms will be those that can improve upon reliable lower-level descriptions in spite of these imperfections. We introduce a dual-space nonorthogonal configuration-interaction (DS-NOCI) framework built around this principle. Rather than replacing a classically accessible NOCI reference manifold with correlated quantum states, DS-NOCI retains both spaces and couples them variationally. The reference sector provides a stable many-body backbone, while the quantum states contribute whatever additional correlation directions they contain. With exact matrix elements, the enlarged dual space gives a ground-state energy no higher than either the reference-only NOCI or correlated-only quantum-NOCI spaces, ensuring that an incomplete correlation model cannot degrade the underlying variational description. The additional reference--correlated matrix elements require only one correlated state preparation and are therefore less demanding than the correlated--correlated block already required by quantum variant of NOCI. Molecular benchmarks further show enhanced resilience to imperfect amplitudes and noisy matrix elements. DS-NOCI thus provides a general strategy for building quantum many-body formulations that remain useful when both correlation models and quantum computations are necessarily incomplete and noisy.

title: Data-Optimized Contingency Screening: A Machine Learning Approach to Power System Security
abstract: Ensuring the security of the power system is essential for stability and reliability, especially in the event of disruption. Effective classification of contingency in power systems enables proactive decision-making and mitigates large-scale breakdowns and failures. This study explores the use of machine learning algorithms to classify security levels of contingencies in power systems into safe, moderate or severe classes. For this approach, Newton-Raphson load flow method extracts system data from contingency scenarios, using Overall Performance Index (OPI) as safety measure. For data pre-processing, Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is used to address class imbalance and reduce dimensionality, respectively. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) is trained and evaluated on datasets generated through N-k contingency scenarios for k equal 1, 2, and 3 on IEEE-14 and IEEE-30 bus systems using four hybrid pre-processing configurations: normalized, SMOTE-balanced, PCA-transformed, and a combined SMOTE PCA-transformed. Performance is assessed by precision, recall and F1 score, with priority given to the severe contingency classes. The RF achieved the highest F1 scores of 0.97 in IEEE-30 and 0.86 in IEEE-14, SVM benefits significantly from PCA and improves the accuracy of the classification, while KNN is best suited for SMOTE and PCA conversion. The findings show that PCA contributes more than SMOTE to the overall performance of the model. However, SMOTE improves recall but can introduce false positives and is therefore a compromise of accuracy. This study highlights machine learning as a scalable and powerful alternative to traditional contingency analysis, which improves the assessment of security in real time.

title: Five-Dimensional Compatibility and Stratified Local-Unitary Structure of Pure Three-Qubit States
abstract: We investigates the joint compatibility problem of the three pairwise concurrences, the three-tangle, and the Kempe invariant in arbitrary pure three-qubit states, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for these five quantities to be simultaneously realizable by the same pure state. This five-dimensional compatibility region can be viewed as a fiber structure over the previously derived four-dimensional reachable region. We further find that the residual continuous local-unitary freedom depends on the position of the state within this region. In the generic interior, one continuous degree of freedom remains. It is fixed if the three-tangle vanishes or a pairwise concurrence becomes zero, and also at the boundary of the four-dimensional tangle region. The Kempe invariant gives the simplest algebraic parametrization of the fifth coordinate, but the same degree of freedom may be described by a known pure-state entanglement monotone. The compatibility conditions can also be expressed in terms of concurrence-based bipartite measures and multipartite quantities fixed by the pairwise concurrences and the three-tangle.

title: When Minute-Resolution Monitoring Meets Session-Level Injury Labels: Landmark-Based Discrimination in Elite Women's Football
abstract: Minute-resolution athlete monitoring is increasingly common, while injury annotation may exist only at the athlete-session level and omit within-session onset time. Replicating a positive session label across every recorded minute would therefore create unsupported minute-level supervision. We address this label-resolution mismatch using fixed elapsed-time landmarks at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 min, constructing one representation per athlete-session from information available up to each landmark while keeping the target as a same-day injury-associated session indicator. Using 2020 SoccerMon data from elite women's football, the modelling cohort contains 2,259 Team A athlete-sessions from 27 athletes, including all 22 positive sessions from five athletes. Evaluation is athlete-disjoint. We compare contextual, cumulative, and dynamic representations; Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and TabPFN; and training-only NONE, SMOTE, and CTGAN conditions. Robustness is assessed using athlete-cluster bootstrap, a fixed common cohort, alternative fold allocations, leave-one-positive-athlete-out analysis, and equal-athlete weighting. Discrimination is landmark-dependent and non-monotonic. TabPFN improves later-landmark discrimination relative to Logistic Regression but does not consistently outperform Random Forest. Synthetic augmentation provides condition-specific rather than universal benefit. The contribution is a unit-aligned framework for using minute-resolution predictors with session-level supervision, not minute-specific injury prediction.

title: Random mixtures in Bayes Hilbert spaces
abstract: We present a framework for the analysis and unmixing of random density mixtures in the Bayes Hilbert space. General identifiability results for mixtures in Hilbert spaces are established and applied to the Bayes Hilbert space setting. Building on these results, we propose a penalised maximum likelihood approach for the unmixing of Bayes Hilbert mixtures aimed at recovering the statistically space-efficient representation, together with a computationally efficient coordinate-wise maximisation algorithm for its implementation. The methodology is illustrated through a hyperspectral data application, where observations can be naturally embedded in the Bayes Hilbert space and analyzed in terms of distributional shape rather than amplitude. A complementary simulation study demonstrates the interpretability and practical performance of the proposed approach.

title: EPIC: Explicit Posterior Item Conditioning for Semantic ID Diffusion Recommendation
abstract: Semantic ID (SID) generative recommendation predicts the next item by generating a short tuple of discrete tokens. Recent masked-diffusion methods improve this process through bidirectional context and flexible decoding, yet recommendation ultimately requires selecting among complete catalog items. At each denoising step, a partial SID can correspond to multiple feasible items, while existing methods primarily reason through position-wise token predictions. We propose Explicit Posterior Item Conditioning (EPIC), which introduces explicit item-level competition into SID denoising. EPIC constructs a personalized posterior over feasible candidate items using the current generation context and the user's recent interactions, then projects this distribution back to unresolved SID positions to guide subsequent token decisions. The pretrained backbone remains frozen and requires no additional decoder forward pass. Experiments on four Amazon benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines, while diagnostic analyses indicate that the gains primarily arise from personalized transition evidence that preserves promising item hypotheses during denoising.

title: AI, Quantum Computing and High-Performance Computing
abstract: The intersection of AI, quantum computing (QC) and high-performance computing (HPC) creates a spectrum of opportunities. AI is already enhancing QC by assisting with the design and performance of quantum hardware and algorithms, while QC offers the potential to address limitations in classical AI by, for example, improving machine learning and model training. This CETaS Snapshot Report assesses the near-term opportunities provided by hybrid quantum-classical computing systems, and the implications for national security and prosperity. The report outlines a number of challenges and recommendations for the UK’s integration of QC and HPC systems, calling for an acceleration of efforts in order to avoid falling behind in an area central to the future of supercomputing.

title: Quantum Adaptive Parameter Tuning for Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing promises transformative advancements across diverse fields, but its practical implementation faces significant hurdles, primarily concerning error correction and computational complexity. This paper investigates a novel approach to mitigate these challenges – Quantum Adaptive Parameter Tuning (QAPT). QAPT leverages the inherent properties of quantum mechanics, specifically the quantum state's sensitivity to noise and errors, to dynamically adjust quantum computation parameters. We propose a sophisticated algorithm that utilizes the security guarantees of quantum mechanics to iteratively refine parameters, minimizing errors and ultimately enhancing computational precision. The core mechanism centers around exploiting the quantum state's response to perturbations to achieve a more accurate outcome. This research explores the potential of QAPT to overcome limitations inherent in current quantum computing architectures, offering a pathway towards more robust and efficient computation.

title: 基于动态矩阵的量子计算的优化算法
abstract: Quantum computing holds tremendous promise for revolutionizing various fields, from drug discovery and materials science to financial modeling and cryptography. However, realizing this potential faces significant challenges, including the need for efficient quantum algorithms and robust error correction. This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on dynamic matrices, designed to address these challenges by automating the adjustment of quantum bit (qubit) states. The proposed algorithm leverages matrix operations to optimize quantum circuit design and minimize errors, ultimately leading to enhanced computational efficiency and precision. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary results, highlighting its potential to significantly accelerate the development and deployment of quantum algorithms.

title: Adaptive Genetic Algorithm Optimization Strategy
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive genetic algorithm optimization strategy designed to enhance the performance of genetic algorithms by dynamically adjusting the algorithm's parameters and selection during the optimization process. The core mechanism centers on a feedback loop that leverages data characteristics to dynamically adjust the genetic algorithm's configuration, significantly improving efficiency. We present a framework that adapts to changing data patterns, enabling the algorithm to converge faster and achieve better solutions. The paper details the implementation of this strategy and provides a comparative analysis of its performance against traditional optimization techniques.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning Loss Function Adjustment Strategy
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive machine learning loss function adjustment strategy, designed to enhance model generalization by dynamically adjusting the weights of the loss function based on data features. Traditional loss function tuning methods often lack this adaptability, leading to suboptimal performance across different datasets and configurations. We propose a novel framework that leverages self-adaptive machine learning techniques to iteratively refine the loss function's parameters, optimizing for improved predictive accuracy and robustness. title: Neural Network Dynamics Modeling via Nonlinear Spatiotemporal Dynamics
abstract: This paper investigates the modeling of neural networks using nonlinear spatiotemporal dynamics. Traditional approaches to neural network modeling often suffer from simplification, failing to accurately capture the intricate dynamic behaviors exhibited by real neural networks. This work proposes a framework based on nonlinear spatiotemporal differential equations to represent the interactions between neurons within a network. The core of this approach involves introducing time-varying parameters and nonlinear functions to construct a dynamic model that explicitly captures the network's spatial and temporal evolution. The efficacy of the proposed model is validated through numerical simulations. The key contribution lies in providing a more detailed and accurate representation, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of neural network dynamics. The model presented here allows for the investigation of complex network behaviors that were previously inaccessible using simpler methodologies.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Modal Information Fusion
abstract: This paper explores the application of multi-modal information fusion to enhance the performance and robustness of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). Current DRL algorithms predominantly rely on single-modality data, limiting their ability to handle complex and uncertain environments. This research proposes a novel framework that integrates information from diverse modalities – including vision, audio, and tactile – to create a richer and more comprehensive representation of the environment. The core mechanism involves a multi-modal fusion algorithm that combines these disparate data streams, leading to improved state estimation and ultimately, better policy learning. We demonstrate, through a theoretical analysis and conceptual design, the potential for significant advancements in DRL systems operating in scenarios with incomplete or noisy information. The key contributions lie in the strategic integration of multi-modal data and its impact on the learning process, moving beyond the limitations of unimodal approaches.

title: Non-Homogeneous Quantum Computing Resource Allocation Optimization
abstract: This paper addresses the critical challenge of resource allocation in non-homogeneous quantum computing environments, where quantum bits (qubits) exhibit significantly varying characteristics. We propose a novel reinforcement learning-based algorithm for optimizing resource allocation, specifically designed to identify the optimal execution path for quantum computing tasks and maximize qubit utilization. The core of our approach lies in building a probabilistic model representing the quantum computing environment and employing a reinforcement learning agent to learn the best qubit allocation strategy through trial and error. This algorithm overcomes the limitations of existing methods that assume uniform qubit properties, leading to improved efficiency and success rates in quantum computations. The algorithm's core equation is as follows: * *E* = ∑i=1K *ri* (1 - *pi*) where *E* represents the overall execution efficiency, *K* is the number of qubits, *ri* is the allocated resource for qubit *i*, and *pi* is the probability of failure for qubit *i*. The algorithm's objective is to minimize *E*. Furthermore, the reward function is defined as: * R = (1 - E)* where *R* is the reward and *E* is the execution efficiency. The algorithm learns by maximizing this reward. The probabilistic model incorporates qubit characteristics such as coherence time, gate fidelity, and coupling strength, represented as probability distributions. The reinforcement learning agent utilizes a Q-learning algorithm to estimate the optimal Q-values, representing the expected reward for each state-action pair. The state space includes qubit characteristics and task requirements, while the action space consists of qubit allocation decisions. The algorithm iteratively updates its Q-values based on observed rewards, converging towards the optimal resource allocation strategy. We demonstrate that this approach offers a significant improvement over traditional uniform qubit allocation methods, particularly in scenarios with highly heterogeneous qubit populations. The primary contribution of this work is the integration of probabilistic modeling and reinforcement learning to effectively address the complexities of non-homogeneous quantum computing.

title: Relational Reasoning via Probabilistic Logic Programming
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to relational reasoning in artificial intelligence by integrating probabilistic logic programming with deep learning techniques. The core idea is to train a deep neural network to learn the parameters of a probabilistic logic program. This allows the system to perform reasoning about relationships between entities, leveraging the expressive power of logic programming for representing complex relational knowledge and the efficiency of deep learning for parameter estimation and inference. We demonstrate that this combined approach can effectively address complex relational reasoning tasks, bridging the traditional divide between symbolic and connectionist AI paradigms. The system learns to represent relational rules probabilistically, enabling it to handle uncertainty and incomplete information inherent in real-world relational data. This work provides a foundational framework for building more robust and flexible AI systems capable of reasoning about relationships in diverse domains. ---

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum topology search algorithm based on adaptive chaos. The algorithm leverages dynamic chaos to efficiently explore complex topological spaces, enabling the discovery of specific quantum topology structures and enhancing quantum information storage and transmission. Traditional topological search methods are often static, limiting their ability to handle intricate environments. Our approach utilizes adaptive chaos to create intelligent search trajectories, offering a promising pathway towards improved quantum information management. This work explores the potential of this method to uncover unique topological properties and facilitate advanced quantum technologies.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Graph Embeddings via Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: Existing self-supervised learning methods for graph embeddings often rely on heuristic approaches without a robust theoretical underpinning. This work introduces a novel framework for learning graph embeddings based on contrastive predictive coding (CPC). The core idea is to train a neural network to predict future graph states given their past states, utilizing a contrastive loss function to promote similarity between embeddings of structurally similar graphs. This approach offers a more principled and stable learning process compared to existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a theoretical analysis and outline the key components and operational details. The primary contribution lies in establishing a clear connection between predictive modeling and graph embedding learning, providing a foundation for future research in this area. The proposed method aims to generate embeddings that capture the underlying structural information of graphs effectively, ultimately improving performance in downstream graph-related tasks. ---

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning by integrating the strengths of logic programming and Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Traditional logic programming systems struggle with uncertainty and noisy data, hindering their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. This work addresses this limitation by employing BNNs to represent the probabilistic aspects of logical rules and facts, enabling reasoning under incomplete and uncertain conditions. Markov Logic Networks (MLNs) are utilized to formally define the probabilistic dependencies between logical predicates. The core innovation lies in the synergistic combination of deductive logic with the probabilistic inference capabilities of BNNs, offering a more robust and adaptable reasoning framework. This framework allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge and the continuous updating of beliefs based on observed evidence. The presented system demonstrates improved performance compared to traditional logic programming approaches when dealing with ambiguous or imprecise information, suggesting a promising direction for intelligent systems in domains where uncertainty is inherent. The system's architecture provides a flexible platform for incorporating diverse knowledge sources and adapting to evolving data.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Modeling Social Influence in Online Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling social influence within online networks. The core argument is that GNNs, with their ability to learn representations from graph-structured data, offer a superior approach compared to traditional methods for predicting information diffusion and user behavior. We construct a graph representation of online social networks, where nodes represent users and edges represent the influence relationships between them. A GNN is then trained to learn node embeddings that encapsulate the network topology and user attributes. These learned embeddings are subsequently utilized to predict the spread of information, user actions, or other relevant outcomes. The presented framework provides a robust and scalable solution for analyzing and forecasting complex social dynamics in online environments. We demonstrate the potential of GNNs to capture the nuanced interactions that drive information propagation and user decision-making, ultimately leading to improved prediction accuracy.

title: Self-Organizing Graph Representations for Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to constructing and refining knowledge graphs (KGs) utilizing a self-organizing mechanism inspired by biological neural networks. Traditional KG construction often relies heavily on manual curation and predefined schemas, limiting adaptability and scalability. Our method leverages a distributed learning algorithm where nodes within the KG iteratively update their representations based on the similarity of their neighbors. This dynamic process leads to the emergent formation of clusters and relationships, effectively allowing the KG to adapt to new information and evolve its structure over time. We introduce the concept of "Self-Organizing Graph Representations" (SOGR) and detail the algorithmic framework, highlighting its potential to overcome the limitations of static KGs and create more robust and nuanced representations of knowledge. The core claim is that KGs can be constructed and refined through a self-organizing process. The core mechanism is a distributed learning algorithm. This approach represents a significant shift towards dynamically evolving KGs, offering a pathway to handle the complexities and uncertainties inherent in real-world knowledge domains. ---

title: Bayesian Network Resonance for Computational Complexity
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian Network Resonance (BNR) to dynamically model and optimize computational complexity. Traditional Bayesian Networks often struggle with complex, evolving systems due to static assumptions and limited adaptability. We propose a novel BNR framework that incorporates continuous, oscillating feedback between nodes, enabling the system to 'resonate' with its own internal state and identify hidden dependencies through dynamic resonance. This allows for a more flexible and potentially more efficient approach to optimization compared to static Bayesian Network models. The core mechanism focuses on creating a system that actively seeks out and mitigates the impact of these hidden dependencies, ultimately leading to improved computational performance. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in a simplified computational complexity setting.

title: 拓扑结构下的量子态生成算法
abstract: Quantum state generation algorithms are a crucial component of quantum computing, enabling the creation and manipulation of complex quantum states. Traditional approaches often rely on predefined patterns, limiting the potential for novel quantum states. This paper introduces a novel quantum state generation algorithm that leverages the inherent structure of quantum topology to dynamically adjust quantum state parameters, mitigating local optima and enabling error range self-adaptation. We propose a mechanism termed "Quantum Topology State Adjustment" (QTSA) which connects the quantum topology structure to the state generation process, dynamically adjusting parameters to explore the full state space. This approach offers a fundamentally new approach to quantum state generation, potentially unlocking new capabilities in quantum information processing. The core claim is that this algorithm generates quantum states exhibiting complex topology and achieves superior quantum information processing capabilities compared to existing methods.

abstract: Time-Encoded Multi-Particle Dynamics (TEMPD) represents a novel approach to modeling dynamic biological systems by encoding time-dependent quantum states within particle interactions. TEMPD's potential lies in its ability to capture subtle temporal dynamics often overlooked in conventional simulations, providing a robust foundation for understanding and potentially guiding biological evolution.

title: Interpretable machine learning model for predicting the ICU readmission of patients after coronary intervention
abstract: To develop and validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model integrated with inflammatory indicators for predicting ICU readmission in patients after coronary intervention (PCI/CABG). We used retrospective data from MIMIC-IV (training, 2196 patients) and MIMIC-III (external validation, 1717 patients). Patients aged > 18 years with complete hematological data and < 40% missing data were included in the study. LASSO regression selected 20 clinical variables; nine ML algorithms (e.g., RF, XGBoost) were compared. The optimal model was evaluated using AUC, calibration curves, DCA, and CIC, with SHAP for interpretability. In MIMIC-IV, 674 (30.7%) patients had multiple ICU admissions, and 440 (25.6%) in MIMIC-III. RF outperformed the other models (internal AUC = 0.85, external AUC = 0.706), with balanced accuracy (0.772), sensitivity (0.748), and specificity (0.795). The key predictors included MLR, maximum creatinine levels, invasive procedures, and so on. The model was optimized for 12 variables and deployed online. The RF model achieves moderate predictive performance for ICU readmission risk of post-coronary intervention patients within the same single tertiary hospital across different periods, and SHAP improves model interpretability to facilitate screening high-risk patients. SHAP enhances interpretability, aiding in the early identification of high-risk patients and improving outcomes.

title: Lattice: Enabling Scalable Enclaves for Commercial RISC-V Platforms
abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have been extensively adopted to facilitate various security-critical applications. However, in stark contrast to well-established TEE technologies such as Intel SGX, AMD SEV, and ARM TrustZone, the adoption within the emerging RISC-V architecture has seen limited traction. Specifically, existing TEE implementations on current commercial RISC-V hardware face two primary constraints. On one hand, most approaches rely on specific hardware extensions or software firmware, hindering their practicality on real platforms. On the other hand, the intrinsic limits of RISC-V’s Physical Memory Protection (PMP) registers, a key hardware mechanism to achieve memory isolation, have significantly restricted the scalability of these designs. To address the above limitations, in this article, we introduce Lattice , a novel RISC-V TEE framework that enables scalable enclaves on commercial RISC-V platforms with a minimal Trusted Computing Base (TCB). Firstly, for enhanced compatibility and portability, Lattice does not rely on any additional hardware extensions and proposes a non-intrusive Secure Monitor (SM) design for the underlying firmware. Secondly, to fully utilize the system’s available memory, Lattice leverages the Dynamic Physical Memory Permission (DPMP) design to enable the execution of enclaves with non-contiguous physical memory, and decouples the management of enclaves to minimize the size of the TCB. Finally, we evaluate the performance of Lattice under various workloads, including file system I/O, databases, web servers, large language models (LLMs), and different system loads. The experimental results indicate that Lattice achieves performance comparable to other TEE systems.

title: A Reverse Sign Language Dictionary: Open-Vocabulary Sign Recognition from Continuous Signing via Video Captioning and Description Retrieval
abstract: Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) is conventionally cast as closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen in training and ties every deployment to a gloss-annotated lexicon. We instead recognize signs extracted from continuous signing by (1) captioning a sign-level clip into a free-form procedural description of the articulation with an open-weight vision-language model, and (2) retrieving the closest entry from a vocabulary of target descriptions with a multilingual sentence encoder: a reverse sign language dictionary that needs no gloss supervision and admits an open vocabulary. On 1,300 sign-level segments from a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) dialogue corpus annotated with procedural descriptions (against a 2% top-10 chance floor over the 503-entry target vocabulary), fine-tuning the captioner substantially improves seen-class retrieval: language and vision tower fine-tuning raises top-10 retrieval on seen classes from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of the three test sets where a closed-set classifier can be evaluated at all. More importantly, unseen-class retrieval also improves significantly over the untrained pipeline (11.5% -> 21.0% top-10, p=0.0094), a regime in which the closed-set classifier cannot participate. A matcher-side empirical upper-bound analysis shows the sentence encoder already recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, locating a gap in captioning quality that we aim to address in future work. To our knowledge this is the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first for JSL.

title: Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion
abstract: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

title: Risk and Anomaly Identification for Distribution Network Optimal Operation Based on Reinforcement Learning and Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Reliable operation of modern distribution networks requires timely identification of operational risks and anomalous events under pervasive uncertainty. In practice, operators must identify risks that are inherent in stochastic yet in-distribution conditions, and anomalies that correspond to out-of-distribution behaviors such as unusual load patterns, extreme weather or cyber-physical attacks. This paper addresses this joint risk and anomaly identification problem for optimal distribution network operation and proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework that is explicitly uncertainty aware. We integrate distributional and Bayesian deep reinforcement learning to realize a second- order uncertainty quantification scheme that decomposes total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, which are respectively used to characterize inherent risk and out-of- distribution anomalies. The resulting epistemic estimates drive both exploration during training and out-of-distribution detec- tion with fallback control during deployment, whereas aleatoric estimates are used to characterize intrinsic operational risk. Simulation results demonstrate the performance of our DRL agent and the effectiveness of the uncertainty quantification.

title: Algorithmic Fractal Resonance (AFR)
abstract: This paper presents Algorithmic Fractal Resonance (AFR), a novel algorithm designed to optimize the performance of neural networks through the integration of fractal geometry and complex resonance. We explore a self-organizing process where the network's weights are iteratively refined to induce resonant patterns, ultimately enhancing learning accuracy and reducing overfitting. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a fractal structure that dynamically adjusts to the network's internal state, amplifying key learning signals. This approach offers a departure from traditional gradient descent optimization, promising improved efficiency and accuracy.

title: Non-linear Topological Structures of Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental properties of quantum entanglement within non-linear topological structures. We propose a novel approach to quantum entanglement computation, leveraging the intricate interplay between topology and quantum mechanics. The core mechanism centers on constructing a computational model predicated on the inherent properties of these structures, allowing for the efficient manipulation and processing of entangled quantum states. This research explores the potential for significant advancements in quantum information processing by embracing a fundamentally different perspective on entanglement. The core claim is that this methodology offers a pathway to overcome limitations of traditional quantum algorithms, particularly those involving large-scale entanglement, offering a robust framework for tackling complex quantum problems. The paper will detail the design of a specific model, highlighting its mathematical foundations and illustrating its potential applications.

title: Quantum Resonance-Based Computational Geometry
abstract: Quantum Resonance-Based Computational Geometry presents a novel approach to geometric computation utilizing quantum entanglement to generate and manipulate geometric patterns. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to create stable, computationally efficient algorithms compared to traditional methods. We detail the core mechanism, focusing on the creation of entangled geometric primitives and their subsequent application within a quantum computing framework. The research investigates the advantages of this methodology, highlighting enhanced stability, faster computation, and the potential for novel geometric patterns. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions and emphasizing the significance of this approach for both fundamental research and potential applications in materials science and design.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Geometric Mapping
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) represents a paradigm shift in computational science, leveraging quantum mechanics to accelerate algorithms and solve previously intractable problems. This paper focuses on a novel approach within QML: Adaptive Geometric Mapping. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the geometric representation of a machine learning model through a self-adaptive process, exploiting the unique quantum properties of states to enhance performance. This methodology aims to overcome limitations of traditional approaches by enabling automated optimization and the exploration of complex solutions. The core mechanism centers around mapping the model's parameters and constraints into a high-dimensional space, guided by quantum algorithms, ultimately leading to improved outcomes. The paper presents a detailed exploration of this framework, including mathematical formulations and illustrative examples demonstrating its potential to surpass existing methods. We will analyze the benefits of this approach in specific machine learning tasks and discuss future research directions.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning Gradient Descent Strategy
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive machine learning gradient descent strategy designed to enhance model precision and efficiency. Traditional gradient descent methods often rely on fixed learning rates and step sizes, failing to effectively adapt to the inherent variability of the data. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts these parameters based on observed data characteristics, leveraging a dynamic learning rate and optimization step size. This approach significantly improves model performance and streamlines the training process. The core mechanism involves integrating a dynamically adjusted learning rate and optimization step size based on feature similarity and gradients, achieving superior results compared to static gradient descent methods. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the proposed strategy, demonstrating its effectiveness through experimental results.

title: Adaptive Distributed Learning with Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Distributed learning (DL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training machine learning models across multiple devices, offering advantages in terms of scalability and reduced communication costs. However, many existing DL approaches operate under the simplifying assumption of identical model parameters and gradients, neglecting the inherent heterogeneity in learner performance and knowledge. This paper introduces a novel adaptive distributed learning framework that explicitly addresses this limitation by incorporating epistemic uncertainty quantification. Each learner estimates its own uncertainty—its lack of knowledge—regarding the global model. This uncertainty is then leveraged to dynamically adjust learning rates and aggregation strategies, prioritizing learners with lower uncertainty. The proposed mechanism promotes more robust and efficient convergence by accounting for learner heterogeneity, leading to a more adaptive and effective distributed learning process. The core claim of this work is that current DL approaches often assume identical model parameters and gradients, ignoring inherent differences in learner performance and knowledge. The core mechanism integrates a mechanism for each learner to estimate *epistemic uncertainty* – its own lack of knowledge – regarding the global model. This uncertainty is then used to dynamically adjust learning rates and aggregation strategies, favouring learners with lower uncertainty. Why it is new is explicitly accounts for learner heterogeneity through uncertainty quantification, leading to more robust and efficient convergence.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Cryptography Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information cryptography algorithm based on the dynamic evolution of quantum states. Traditional cryptographic methods rely on static keys, while this approach leverages the inherent instability of quantum states to generate keys, enhancing security. The algorithm employs a continuous state transformation process to produce a unique key for each input data. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential for robust encryption. The core mechanism centers around the manipulation of quantum states to achieve key generation and decryption.

title: Decentralized Differential Privacy via Byzantine Fault Tolerance Consensus
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to achieving differential privacy in decentralized networks by integrating Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) consensus mechanisms. The core idea revolves around a consensus algorithm where each participating node introduces noise to its data before dissemination, with the noise level dynamically calibrated based on the detected Byzantine behavior of other nodes. This method addresses the challenges of maintaining privacy while operating in environments susceptible to malicious or faulty actors. We demonstrate that by leveraging the robustness of BFT, we can guarantee differential privacy without relying on centralized authorities or requiring strict trust assumptions among network participants. The proposed system provides a practical solution for privacy-preserving data sharing in decentralized settings.

title: Probability Logic and Dynamic Matrix Coupling Analysis
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for coupling analysis in large-scale machine learning models, leveraging the strengths of probability logic and dynamic matrix representations. The core concept is to model data distribution dynamics through a dynamic matrix, which then influences model parameter optimization. We propose a method for iteratively updating the dynamic matrix based on observed data, facilitating the discovery of optimal model parameters and improving overall performance. This approach addresses limitations of traditional techniques by providing a more adaptable and intuitive method for understanding and managing complex model behavior. The framework is designed to be scalable and adaptable to various machine learning tasks.

title: Automated Theorem Proving with Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has achieved significant progress over the years, yet it frequently struggles with complex mathematical reasoning and strategic planning. This work introduces a novel approach to ATP leveraging deep reinforcement learning (DRL). The core idea is to train an intelligent agent capable of interacting with a theorem prover, learning optimal strategies for selecting theorems, axioms, and proof tactics. We hypothesize that a DRL agent can surpass human capabilities by learning a more efficient and robust reasoning process. This paper details the architecture of the agent, the reward function design, and the training methodology. Preliminary results demonstrate the potential of this approach to automate theorem proving effectively, suggesting a new paradigm for tackling challenging mathematical problems. The primary goal is to create an agent that can dynamically adapt to the proof process, improving upon the limitations of traditional, rule-based ATP systems.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Secure Multi-Party Computation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to decentralized federated learning (DFL) that leverages secure multi-party computation (SMPC) to guarantee data privacy during collaborative model training. Traditional federated learning methods, while promoting data sharing for model improvement, inherently expose individual datasets to the central server, raising significant privacy concerns. Our framework addresses this limitation by employing SMPC protocols, enabling model updates to be aggregated securely without revealing the underlying data. This approach provides a strong privacy guarantee, combining the benefits of federated learning with robust privacy protection. We present a detailed description of the system architecture, the SMPC protocols utilized, and the mathematical formulation underpinning the aggregation process. The core claim of this work is the ability to enable collaborative model training across multiple parties without revealing individual data. The core mechanism relies on implementing a federated learning framework based on secure multi-party computation protocols, where model updates are aggregated securely without exposing the underlying data. This research represents a significant advancement in the field of privacy-preserving machine learning.

title: Quantum-Inspired Secure Multi-Party Computation via Tensor Networks
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) aims to enable computation on sensitive data without revealing the individual inputs of the participants. Traditional SMPC protocols often suffer from significant computational overhead, particularly in terms of communication complexity. This paper proposes a novel approach to SMPC leveraging tensor network techniques inspired by quantum computation. We demonstrate that tensor networks can efficiently represent and manipulate the necessary data structures for SMPC protocols, leading to a substantial reduction in communication overhead and improved scalability. Our method utilizes the inherent structure of tensor networks to minimize the number of exchanges required during computation, effectively addressing a key bottleneck in existing SMPC implementations. We outline the theoretical foundations and present a framework for designing SMPC protocols using tensor networks. This work represents a significant step towards practical and efficient SMPC solutions, particularly for large-scale datasets and complex computations. The key contribution lies in the application of quantum-inspired techniques to solve classical computational problems, specifically within the context of secure computation.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Iteration (Qefi)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Iteration (Qefi) proposes a novel method for generating self-similar fractal geometries through the application of quantum entanglement. The core mechanism involves establishing a 'seed' fractal pattern and leveraging entanglement to iteratively refine and explore complex geometries, potentially achieving unprecedented precision and generating highly structured patterns. This approach offers a departure from conventional fractal algorithms, capitalizing on the unique properties of quantum mechanics to unlock new levels of geometric complexity and self-similarity.

title: Variable Quantum Geometry: A Novel Approach to Quantum Computing Optimization
abstract: This research investigates the application of variable quantum geometry (VQG) to enhance the performance of quantum computing systems. We propose a novel quantum geometry model that dynamically adjusts the quantum system's geometry to optimize computational outcomes. The core mechanism involves utilizing VQG to represent and manipulate quantum states, leading to improved fidelity and efficiency in quantum algorithms. This paper presents the foundation of this model and its potential impact on various quantum computing scenarios. We explore the benefits of this approach, focusing on the optimization of quantum circuits and the development of novel quantum algorithms. The core claim is that VQG provides a viable pathway to significantly improve the performance of quantum computation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding: A Probabilistic Modeling Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for information encoding and transmission. This paper explores the potential of utilizing entanglement to develop a probabilistic modeling framework for information exchange, focusing on the design of a computational paradigm predicated on entanglement's non-local properties. We propose a novel approach that leverages entanglement to establish a probabilistic information transfer mechanism and constructs a computational framework inherently sensitive to entanglement. This work aims to investigate the implications of quantum entanglement in securing information and offers a pathway to explore novel cryptographic techniques within the quantum computing landscape.

title: Qubits of a Feather, Flawed Together: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared in the context of Physics. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of quantum computing and qubits as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Physics.
